key_messages: Pockets of freezing rain across northern New York and central and northeastern Vermont will result in slippery travel and localized power outages tonight.

Scattered to numerous power outages are possible near the western slopes of the southern Greens, while isolated outages are possible in other favored downslope areas across northern New York and Vermont, associated with a strong easterly wind event.
No significant weather is expected over the weekend after tonight's storm. Beneficial, light mountain snow accumulation is expected, with primarily rain showers below 2500 feet.
Next chance for precipitation will come Sunday night into Monday as a frontal system crosses our region.

Wind Advisories were expanded into portions of northern New York and northern Vermont. Confidence in freezing rain impacts has further increased in the northern St. Lawrence Valley. Freezing rain potential has increased in portions of central Vermont with colder temperatures at the onset of precipitation than previously expected.

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
318 PM EST Thu Nov 26 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 318 PM EST Thursday...

The Wind Advisory in eastern Rutland County was upgraded to a High 
Wind Warning. Wind Advisories were expanded into portions of 
northern New York and northern Vermont. Confidence in freezing rain 
impacts has further increased in the northern St. Lawrence Valley. 
Freezing rain potential has increased in portions of central Vermont 
with colder temperatures at the onset of precipitation than 
previously expected.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 318 PM EST Thursday...

1. Pockets of freezing rain across northern New York and 
central and northeastern Vermont will result in slippery travel 
and localized power outages tonight. 

2. Scattered to numerous power outages are possible near the 
western slopes of the southern Greens, while isolated outages are 
possible in other favored downslope areas across northern New York 
and Vermont, associated with a strong easterly wind event.

3. No significant weather is expected over the weekend after 
tonight's storm. Beneficial, light mountain snow accumulation is 
expected, with primarily rain showers below 2500 feet.

4. Next chance for precipitation will come Sunday night into 
Monday as a frontal system crosses our region.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 318 PM EST Thursday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: A deep (997 millibar) and large low pressure system 
currently in Virginia will be pulled north-northwestward into 
western Pennsylvania tonight and slightly strengthen. Satellite 
imagery shows a conveyor belt of rich moisture over the western 
Atlantic Ocean being drawn into the northeastern flank of this 
system, which will transport moderate to briefly heavy rainfall 
rates into our region.  

There has been a trend towards a larger footprint of ice 
accumulations within the Winter Weather Advisory area, especially in 
Vermont, as rain falls tonight. One reason is colder than expected 
air temperatures today resulting in road temperatures only reaching 
the middle 30s in much of the area. Mid-afternoon temperatures are 
only in the 30 to 33 range in much of central Vermont, and with 
every degree meaningful for the important freezing point as rain 
reaches the surface, the implications for ice accumulation are 
massive. As of now, we expect wet-bulb cooling at precipitation 
onset being offset by the very strong warm air advection associated 
with the plume of moisture. That being said, the rainfall amounts 
are fairly robust with high probalities of rainfall rates in excess 
of 0.06" concurrent with freezing rain, which is a proxy for 
signficant icing potential.
 
Colder, drier northeasterly flow in the northern St. Lawrence Valley 
could lead to relatively efficient accretion and the majority of 
rain falling in the form of freezing rain. With ice-to-liquid ratios 
closer to 1, there is a high end potential for higher ice amounts 
than forecast which would lead to significant ice, in which power 
outages would occur due to its weight on trees and power lines. 
Meanwhile, the impacts in central Vermont near and east of the Green 
Mountains look relatively small with threat of heavier amounts 
limited to higher terrain with lower population, but travel may be 
difficult with even light ice amounts. Eventually, sometime Friday 
morning, temperatures will warm above freezing with all 
precipitation changing to rain.

KEY MESSAGE 2: The swath of rain will be accompanied by strong easterly 
winds, which mostly will stay above the ground due to very stable 
air. However, we remain concerned for locally damaging winds, and 
confidence in occurence in eastern Rutland County led to an upgrade 
to a High Wind Warning. The 3 kilometer REFS guidance, which can 
simulate downslope winds in complex terrain, shows high statistical 
likelihood of wind gusts exceeding 55 MPH along the western slopes 
in a narrow band which includes a portion of Route 4 just east of 
Mendon and eastern portions of Danby. The timeframe of strongest 
winds remains tricky and the latest guidance shows perhaps a shorter 
window of the strongest winds being situated below inversion height. 
However, a localized, favorably sharp west-east pressure gradient 
should arise in pressure fields towards 10 PM, concurrent with a 70 
knot east-southeast wind field in the 875 to 925 millibar layer just 
above a shallow low level inversion. Cross sections show some 
mountain wave breaking, which would be expected to extend only a 
short distance from our mountain peaks. Therefore, the potential for 
damaging winds currently looks isolated to the more immediate 
western slopes. 

The strongest winds do look concurrent with some of the steadier 
rain, which should limit the duration of any of these winds 
extending farther westward. However, we have expanded Wind 
Advisories across more of our region as well, addressing potential 
for other western slope areas that will be vulnerable to wind 
impacts. Think these areas will see a window after rain ends early 
Friday morning to realize potential for gusty downslope winds; with 
more saturated soils following the rain, relatively unusual 
magnitude of easterly winds, even sub-advisory level, may be capable 
of causing tree damage and result in isolated power outages across 
our region.

KEY MESSAGE 3: 
Low pressure will finally pass through northern New York and 
Vermont Friday evening, leading to a period of widespread 
showers pushing through the area followed by localized upslope 
snow showers. Snow levels look too low to see any snow aside 
from mid-slope areas during this period, but some of our 
mountain summits could do well with much needed natural snow of 
a few to possibly several inches. Precipitation should taper off
Saturday morning. Most of the weekend looks quiet and a bit 
warmer than normal, especially on Sunday when more sunshine is 
expected and low level temperatures tick up a bit.

KEY MESSAGE 4: Sunday night into Monday will bring our next chance for 
any weather as a low pressure system and associated fronts will 
cross our forecast area. Minimal impacts are expected with this 
system as boundary layer temperatures will be mild enough that 
precipitation type will be mainly light rain/rain showers in all but 
the highest elevations. We will be watching the potential for any 
mixed precipitation especially Sunday night as there may be some 
cold air lingering around. There could be a change over to show 
showers as the precipitation comes to an end Monday night, 
especially across the northern higher elevation areas. After maximum 
temperatures on Monday reach the mid 40s to around 50 in the 
afternoon, cold air rushes in behind departing system and lows will 
dip back into the 20s.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z THURSDAY THROUGH TUESDAY/...
Through 18Z Friday...VFR conditions continue at the moment, but
will be lowering as precipitation lifts into our area from the 
south this evening and ceilings lower. Mainly rain showers 
expected at all sites, but will have freezing rain at MSS. With 
light rain dampening SFC winds and a low level jet moving in 
overhead, the LLWS threat will be increasing at the same time as
precipitation spreads northward. Best chances for IFR will be 
after 06Z Friday, but light FZRA could begin 03-06Z at MSS with 
cold air funneling out of the northeast along the St Lawrence 
Valley. SLK will have the threat of FZRA as well, but may hold 
off and be limited to elevations above the terminal. Gustiest 
winds will be at RUT with winds increasing after 15Z and further
after 19Z as winds downslope off the Greens.

Outlook...

Friday Night: Mainly IFR, with areas MVFR possible. Definite
SHRA.
Saturday: Mainly IFR, with areas MVFR possible. Chance SHRA.
Saturday Night: Mainly IFR, with areas MVFR possible. Chance RA.
Sunday: Mainly MVFR, with areas VFR possible. NO SIG WX.
Sunday Night: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. Definite RA.
Monday: Mainly MVFR, with areas IFR possible. Likely RA.
Monday Night: Mainly MVFR, with areas VFR possible. Chance SN.
Tuesday: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. NO SIG WX.

&&
